main.title: Star Wars: Rogue Squadron
main.subtitle: Factor 5 / LucasArts · Nintendo 64
main.summary: Star Wars: Rogue Squadron is Factor 5 and LucasArts' arcade flying game about Luke Skywalker leading Rebel pilots against the Empire. Missions take the squadron across planetary surfaces to attack targets, protect allies, rescue civilians and gather information. The player flies familiar Star Wars craft with different weapons and handling. The emphasis stays on understanding an immediate operation rather than managing a complex cockpit. A vehicle or settlement on the ground can become the reason to turn away from a tempting enemy fighter overhead.

cards.heading: Lead the squadron over a threatened world
cards.text: Star Wars: Rogue Squadron is Factor 5 and LucasArts' arcade flying game about Luke Skywalker leading Rebel pilots against the Empire. Missions take the squadron across planetary surfaces to attack targets, protect allies, rescue civilians and gather information. The player flies familiar Star Wars craft with different weapons and handling. The emphasis stays on understanding an immediate operation rather than managing a complex cockpit. A vehicle or settlement on the ground can become the reason to turn away from a tempting enemy fighter overhead.

cards.heading: The objective determines the flight path
cards.text: Each mission has its own combination of targets and people to defend. Watching the whole situation matters because defeating every visible enemy may leave the important objective exposed. Hidden upgrades improve the available craft, while performance is assessed against medal requirements after the operation. Those goals encourage returning to a known mission with a more efficient route. Familiarity changes the flight from a first attempt at survival into a sequence of deliberate turns, attacks and checks on the allies who still need protection.

cards.heading: A console showcase with a PC companion
cards.text: The Windows edition appeared a few days before the Nintendo 64 version in December 1998. On Nintendo's console, the optional Expansion Pak enabled a higher display resolution. Factor 5 developed the engine and sound technology while LucasArts contributed the story and mission design. The earlier snowspeeder sequence in Shadows of the Empire helped inspire the focus on planetary flight. Rogue Squadron expanded that idea into a complete campaign, later followed by GameCube sequels that carried the squadron's combination of clear objectives and cinematic aerial action onto another generation.

main.title: R4: Ridge Racer Type 4
main.summary: R4: Ridge Racer Type 4, released without the 'R4' prefix in PAL territories, is a 1998 racing video game developed and published by Namco for the PlayStation.

cards.text: R4: Ridge Racer Type 4, released without the 'R4' prefix in PAL territories, is a 1998 racing video game developed and published by Namco for the PlayStation. It is the fourth home title in the Ridge Racer series after Rage Racer (1996) and was initially released on December 3, 1998 in Japan, with global releases following in 1999.

Maintaining the arcade-style gameplay of its predecessors, R4: Ridge Racer Type 4 introduces a new Grand Prix, named Real Racing Roots '99, consisting of four teams that the player may join, with associated sponsorships that can also be chosen, each offering different effects to the driving. Additionally, every team also has its own story mode, accompanied with a manager that interacts with the player during the season. The number of car models was expanded to include over 300 vehicles.

R4: Ridge Racer Type 4 was positively received, with praise for its presentation, art, driving, and soundtrack, though some criticism was directed to its cars' overly light drifting compared to earlier titles in the series. Retrospective reviewers considered it as one of the greatest racing games ever made. The game was later re-released on the PlayStation Network service in 2011, on the PlayStation Classic console in 2018, and in 2023 for PlayStation 4 and PlayStation 5. It was followed by Ridge Racer V in 2000, which moved the series on to next generation hardware.

main.title: Suikoden II
main.subtitle: Two friends on opposite sides
main.summary: Suikoden II is Konami's PlayStation role-playing game, first released in Japan on 17 December 1998. Three years after the original, war between Highland and the City-States of Jowston draws a young soldier and his friend Jowy into opposing responsibilities. Each receives half of the Rune of the Beginning, tying their personal relationship to a larger conflict. Yoshitaka Murayama directed the adventure, with music by Miki Higashino and Keiko Fukami. Recruiting the 108 Stars of Destiny makes the growing resistance a community of people, rather than a party that exists only for the next battle.

cards.heading: Two friends on opposite sides
cards.text: Suikoden II is Konami's PlayStation role-playing game, first released in Japan on 17 December 1998. Three years after the original, war between Highland and the City-States of Jowston draws a young soldier and his friend Jowy into opposing responsibilities. Each receives half of the Rune of the Beginning, tying their personal relationship to a larger conflict. Yoshitaka Murayama directed the adventure, with music by Miki Higashino and Keiko Fukami. Recruiting the 108 Stars of Destiny makes the growing resistance a community of people, rather than a party that exists only for the next battle.

cards.heading: A home built by recruitment
cards.text: The player finds allies through conversations, exploration and small tasks, bringing more than a hundred possible recruits to the cause. Only some fight in the ordinary party; others give the base additional activities and services. The organisation therefore becomes visible through the people who live there. Towns also offer equipment, weapon sharpening and runes, while the surrounding country brings random encounters. Lower-level companions gain experience quickly against stronger enemies, helping newly recruited characters catch up. Choosing a different party becomes practical without requiring every newcomer to repeat the same long training route.

cards.heading: The war changes its scale
cards.text: Ordinary party battles share the adventure with individual duels and larger clashes between armies. Each format gives the conflict a different scale, moving from a personal confrontation to the forces gathered around the protagonist. Runes provide magic and specialised abilities, with limited spell uses asking for planning across encounters. Save data from the first game can alter references and strengthen returning characters, connecting this new war to an earlier journey. Later compilations and the 2025 HD remaster brought the original pair to further hardware.

main.title: Baldur's Gate
main.summary: Baldur's Gate is a 1998 role-playing video game developed by BioWare and published by Interplay Entertainment.

cards.heading: Baldur's Gate
cards.text: Baldur's Gate is a 1998 role-playing video game developed by BioWare and published by Interplay Entertainment. It is the first game in the Baldur's Gate series and takes place in the Forgotten Realms, a high fantasy campaign setting, using a modified version of the Advanced Dungeons & Dragons (AD&D) 2nd edition rules. It was the first game to use the Infinity Engine for its graphics, with Interplay using the engine for other Forgotten Realms-licensed games, including the Icewind Dale series and Planescape: Torment. The game's story focuses on a player-made character who travels across the Sword Coast alongside a party of companions.

cards.heading: Reception and legacy
cards.text: The game received critical acclaim and was credited for revitalizing computer role-playing games. An expansion pack was released titled Tales of the Sword Coast, as were two sequels, Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn (2000) and Baldur's Gate 3 (2023). An enhanced, remastered version of the Infinity Engine was later created as part of Beamdog's Baldur's Gate: Enhanced Edition, the first new release in the franchise in nearly nine years. The original Baldur's Gate continues to be referenced as a point of inspiration in many modern role-playing games, and is often cited as one of the best video games ever made.

main.title: Goemon's Great Adventure
main.subtitle: Konami · Nintendo 64
main.summary: Goemon's Great Adventure is Konami's Nintendo 64 platformer about recovering a stolen resurrection machine and stopping the revived ruler of the underworld. Goemon, Ebisumaru, Sasuke and Yae travel through five worlds filled with monsters, towns and anachronistic machinery. The action follows a side-scrolling path through three-dimensional scenery, allowing the route to bend through the environment while remaining clearly defined. Two players can travel together, giving the familiar comic cast another way to share the work of crossing an obstacle or confronting an enemy.

cards.heading: Another journey through the world of Goemon
cards.text: Goemon's Great Adventure is Konami's Nintendo 64 platformer about recovering a stolen resurrection machine and stopping the revived ruler of the underworld. Goemon, Ebisumaru, Sasuke and Yae travel through five worlds filled with monsters, towns and anachronistic machinery. The action follows a side-scrolling path through three-dimensional scenery, allowing the route to bend through the environment while remaining clearly defined. Two players can travel together, giving the familiar comic cast another way to share the work of crossing an obstacle or confronting an enemy.

cards.heading: A pass is earned through another task
cards.text: An overworld connects stages, settlements and dungeons. Completing levels and helping people in town earns the entry passes needed to reach later destinations. Each character's abilities provide another approach to the platforming, while portals and towns allow a change of companion. The route therefore includes reasons to pause, speak to somebody and attempt a task beyond merely reaching the next stage's exit. Different paths and optional discoveries give the surrounding world more activity than a simple line of levels would provide.

cards.heading: Keep the partner within reach
cards.text: Cooperative players share the visible space, requiring them to make progress together rather than run independently into different parts of the level. That limitation makes agreement about the next jump or enemy useful in itself. Musical themes, Japanese folklore and giant robot encounters preserve the series' exuberant character. Released overseas in 1999, and called Mystical Ninja 2 Starring Goemon in Europe, the game uses the newer console's depth to stage an adventure whose movement remains closely related to the series' earlier side-scrolling outings.

main.title: Sonic Adventure
main.summary: Sonic Adventure is a 1998 platform game developed by Sonic Team and published by Sega for the Dreamcast.

cards.text: Sonic Adventure is a 1998 platform game developed by Sonic Team and published by Sega for the Dreamcast. It was the first main Sonic the Hedgehog game to feature 3D gameplay. It follows Sonic the Hedgehog, Miles "Tails" Prower, Knuckles the Echidna, Amy Rose, Big the Cat, and E-102 Gamma in their quests to collect the Chaos Emeralds and stop Doctor Ivo Robotnik from unleashing Chaos, an ancient evil. Controlling one of the six characters—each with their own abilities—players complete levels to progress the story. Sonic Adventure retains many elements from prior Sonic games, such as power-ups and the ring-based health system. Players can play minigames such as racing and interact with Chao, a virtual pet.

Sonic Team began developing Sonic Adventure in 1997, after the cancellation of the Sega Saturn game Sonic X-treme. Led by director Takashi Iizuka and producer Yuji Naka, the team strove to reinvent Sonic for the 3D era of video games. Adventure features a stronger emphasis on storytelling and role-playing elements in contrast to previous Sonic games, while Yuji Uekawa redesigned the series's characters for their transition to 3D. Sonic Team attempted to demonstrate the technical prowess of the Dreamcast with realistic graphics and drew inspiration from locations in Peru and Guatemala. The soundtrack was primarily composed by Jun Senoue, who preferred rock music over the electropop of previous Sonic games.

Following its reveal at the Tokyo International Forum in August 1998, Sonic Adventure was highly anticipated and was released in Japan in December 1998, North America in September 1999, and Europe in October 1999. It received acclaim and became the Dreamcast's bestseller, with 2.5 million copies sold by August 2006. Reviewers considered Adventure a major technical advancement and praised the visuals and gameplay. Though critics noted glitches and camera problems, and reactions to the audio were mixed, they considered Sonic Adventure exceptional; some speculated that it could help re-establish Sega as the dominant console manufacturer after the unsuccessful Saturn.

Journalists have retrospectively ranked Sonic Adventure among the best Sonic games, and it is recognized as an important release in both the series and the platform genre. Many characters and concepts introduced in Adventure recur in later Sonic games. Sonic Adventure 2 was released in 2001. Adventure was ported to the GameCube and Windows in 2003 with modernized visuals, more challenges and additional content, while a high-definition version was released for the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 in 2010 and for Windows in 2011. Reviews for these releases were less positive; critics felt the game had not aged well and ran at an inconsistent frame rate.

main.title: Bugs Bunny: Lost in Time
main.subtitle: A wrong turn through time
main.summary: Bugs Bunny: Lost in Time moved the rabbit’s cartoon logic into a 3D platform adventure in 1999. Developed by Behaviour Interactive and published by Infogrames for PlayStation, it also received a Windows edition later that year. An accidental encounter with a time machine interrupts a trip to Pismo Beach and leaves Bugs trying to return to his own time.

cards.heading: A wrong turn through time
cards.text: Bugs Bunny: Lost in Time moved the rabbit’s cartoon logic into a 3D platform adventure in 1999. Developed by Behaviour Interactive and published by Infogrames for PlayStation, it also received a Windows edition later that year. An accidental encounter with a time machine interrupts a trip to Pismo Beach and leaves Bugs trying to return to his own time.

cards.heading: Five eras and the clocks between them
cards.text: Merlin Munroe introduces the basic movements in Nowhere before the journey opens into five eras, from the Stone Age to Dimension X. Clocks unlock further destinations, while carrots restore energy and golden carrots help open hidden areas. Returning to an era with new possibilities makes the journey more than a straight sequence of levels.

cards.heading: Cartoon tricks in three dimensions
cards.text: Bugs can sneak, kick, manipulate objects, tunnel through rabbit holes and use his ears to slow a fall. Those actions turn familiar cartoon tricks into practical solutions for navigating space and outwitting opponents. Elmer Fudd, Witch Hazel, Yosemite Sam and Marvin the Martian provide recognizable antagonists, with each encounter placed within the game’s changing historical scenery.

main.title: Disney's Tarzan
main.subtitle: Growing up among the branches
main.summary: Eurocom’s Disney’s Tarzan arrived on Windows and PlayStation in 1999, following the animated film’s hero from childhood into adult adventures. The jungle is built in three dimensions, while much of the platforming action is viewed from the side. Running and jumping are joined by climbing, swinging on vines and sliding along branches. Rather than making the forest a static backdrop, these movements turn its trees, slopes and gaps into the route itself. A Nintendo 64 edition followed in 2000.

cards.heading: From childhood to the rescue
cards.text: Eurocom’s Disney’s Tarzan arrived on Windows and PlayStation in 1999, following the animated film’s hero from childhood into adult adventures. The jungle is built in three dimensions, while much of the platforming action is viewed from the side. Running and jumping are joined by climbing, swinging on vines and sliding along branches. Rather than making the forest a static backdrop, these movements turn its trees, slopes and gaps into the route itself. A Nintendo 64 edition followed in 2000.

cards.heading: Reading the jungle through movement
cards.text: Fruit projectiles give Tarzan a way to deal with enemies at a distance, while collectibles encourage detours beyond the most obvious path. Tokens, the letters of his name and sketch pieces make the stages places to search as well as traverse. Familiar characters and situations connect the movement challenges to Tarzan’s changing relationships with the jungle and the human visitors. The original credits distinguish the film’s musical material, associated with Phil Collins and Mark Mancina, from the game music arranged and recorded by Steve Duckworth. The result is an adaptation whose identity lies as much in the rhythm of moving through the forest as in recreating the film’s images.

main.title: Dance Dance Revolution Controller
main.subtitle: The controller moves to the floor
main.summary: Konami's soft dance mat brought PlayStation rhythm games under your feet in 1999.

cards.heading: Step into the rhythm
cards.text: The PlayStation version of Dance Dance Revolution reached Japan in 1999 with a soft dance mat as a dedicated accessory. Its four directional panels turned the scrolling arrows on television into steps on the floor, bringing the arcade game's central idea into the living room.

cards.heading: An arcade idea at home
cards.text: The mat connected to the console's controller port and included controls such as Start and Select. Timing became a movement of the whole body rather than a press of the thumb. Different compatible mats and regional designs followed; the home accessory was distinct from the arcade machine's rigid metal platform.

main.title: Prince of Persia 3D
main.subtitle: The Prince enters three dimensions
main.summary: Prince of Persia 3D brought the series to a fully three-dimensional world on Windows in 1999, developed by Red Orb Entertainment and published under The Learning Company.

cards.heading: The Prince enters three dimensions
cards.text: Prince of Persia 3D brought the series to a fully three-dimensional world on Windows in 1999, developed by Red Orb Entertainment and published under The Learning Company. A diplomatic visit to King Assan ends with the Prince imprisoned and separated from his wife. Escaping means reading spaces from behind the character: judging ledges, climbing, avoiding traps and fighting with melee weapons or a bow. The original manual teaches directional attacks, blocks and feints rather than treating combat as a single repeated strike. Its illustrated pages also preserve the designs for the Prince, his enemies and their architectural world.

cards.heading: A different path for the series
cards.text: Jordan Mechner served as a consultant. In a firsthand retrospective published in October 2026, he described an internal Red Orb production led by Andrew Pedersen and explained that his story work concentrated on tightening the cinematic sequences. Building a new 3D development pipeline amid changes of corporate ownership complicated the work. The game consequently marks a distinct experiment between the earlier side-view adventures and Ubisoft’s later Sands of Time series. Its original manual credits Tom Rettig for music and design, with further music credits for Jonelle Adkisson and Greg Rahn.
